```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(selectiveHotelling)
set.seed(1)
```

## The problem

It is common to *cluster* a dataset and then ask whether two of the discovered
clusters really differ in their means. The trouble is that k-means has already
used the data to carve out the most-separated grouping, so a standard
two-sample test applied to those clusters is testing a hypothesis that was
chosen *because* the data looked separated. The resulting p-values are
anti-conservative: they reject far too often, even when there is no true
structure.

`selectiveHotelling` fixes this for the two-sample Hotelling $T^2$ test with an
**unknown** covariance matrix. It computes a Monte Carlo p-value whose null
reference distribution conditions on the k-means selection event, so the
selective Type I error is controlled.

This vignette:

1. Shows that the **naive** Hotelling p-value is anti-conservative on null data.
2. Shows that `selective_hotelling_test()` is **calibrated** on the same data.
3. Gives a brief **power** illustration on data with genuinely separated
   clusters.

All chunks are kept deliberately small (short MCMC runs, few replicates) so the
vignette builds quickly; for real analyses use more burn-in, more draws, and
more replicates.

## A global-null dataset

We draw exchangeable (equicorrelated) Gaussian data in which **every**
observation shares the same mean. Any apparent cluster separation is therefore
spurious -- this is the null we want a valid test to respect.

```{r one-dataset}
dat <- generate_exchangeable_null_data(n = 30, p = 2, rho = 0.2)
X <- dat$dat
cl <- kmeans_fun(X, k = 3)$cluster
table(cl)
```

## The naive Hotelling p-value

The classical two-sample Hotelling $T^2$ converts to an $F$ statistic via

$$
F = \frac{n_1 + n_2 - p - 1}{p\,(n_1 + n_2 - 2)}\; T^2,
\qquad
F \sim F_{p,\; n_1 + n_2 - p - 1}
$$

under a (fixed, pre-specified) null. The function below returns that naive
p-value. It is exactly what you would get from a textbook test that ignores the
clustering.

```{r naive-fun}
naive_hotelling_p <- function(X, cl, k1, k2) {
  n1 <- sum(cl == k1); n2 <- sum(cl == k2); p <- ncol(X)
  T2 <- hotelling_T2(X, cl, k1, k2)
  if (!is.finite(T2) || (n1 + n2 - p - 1) < 1) return(NA_real_)
  Fstat <- (n1 + n2 - p - 1) / (p * (n1 + n2 - 2)) * T2
  stats::pf(Fstat, df1 = p, df2 = n1 + n2 - p - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
}
```

We also need a small helper to pick a pair of clusters that is large enough to
test (each cluster needs at least a couple of members, and the pooled
covariance must be invertible).

```{r pick-pair}
pick_pair <- function(X, cl) {
  labs <- as.integer(names(which(table(cl) >= 3)))
  if (length(labs) < 2) return(NULL)
  combs <- utils::combn(labs, 2)
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(combs))) {
    if (is.finite(hotelling_T2(X, cl, combs[1, j], combs[2, j]))) {
      return(c(combs[1, j], combs[2, j]))
    }
  }
  NULL
}
```

On our single null dataset the naive p-value is typically tiny, even though
there is no real difference in means:

```{r naive-one}
pr <- pick_pair(X, cl)
naive_hotelling_p(X, cl, pr[1], pr[2])
```

### Naive p-values are anti-conservative across replicates

Repeating over several null datasets, the naive p-values cluster near zero
instead of being spread uniformly over `[0, 1]`. A valid test would reject a
null at level 0.05 only about 5% of the time; the naive test rejects almost
always.

```{r naive-reps}
n_rep <- 15
naive_p <- rep(NA_real_, n_rep)
for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {
  Xr  <- generate_exchangeable_null_data(n = 30, p = 2, rho = 0.2)$dat
  clr <- kmeans_fun(Xr, k = 3)$cluster
  prr <- pick_pair(Xr, clr)
  if (!is.null(prr)) naive_p[r] <- naive_hotelling_p(Xr, clr, prr[1], prr[2])
}
summary(naive_p)
mean(naive_p <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)   # should be ~0.05 for a valid test
```

The mean is far below 0.5 and the rejection rate is far above 0.05: the naive
test is badly anti-conservative after clustering.

## The selective Hotelling p-value

`selective_hotelling_test()` instead simulates the null reference distribution
*conditional on the selection event* by sampling the polar factor $Q$ uniformly
over the part of the Stiefel manifold consistent with the observed cluster
pair. Because the polar factor is uniform on the manifold regardless of the
unknown covariance $\Sigma$, the resulting p-value is valid without estimating
or knowing $\Sigma$.

We use the supported `condition_on = "final"` path (the default) and short MCMC
settings for speed.

```{r selective-one}
res <- selective_hotelling_test(
  X, k1 = pr[1], k2 = pr[2], K = 3,
  sampler = "fast",
  burn = 200, B = 400, thin = 2
)
print(res)
```

### Selective p-values are calibrated across replicates

Running the same replicate loop with the selective test, the p-values are now
spread across `[0, 1]` with a mean near 0.5, and the level-0.05 rejection rate
is in the right ballpark (small-sample Monte Carlo noise aside).

```{r selective-reps}
n_rep <- 15
sel_p <- rep(NA_real_, n_rep)
for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {
  Xr  <- generate_exchangeable_null_data(n = 30, p = 2, rho = 0.2)$dat
  clr <- kmeans_fun(Xr, k = 3)$cluster
  prr <- pick_pair(Xr, clr)
  if (is.null(prr)) next
  sel_p[r] <- tryCatch(
    selective_hotelling_test(
      Xr, prr[1], prr[2], K = 3, sampler = "fast",
      burn = 200, B = 400, thin = 2
    )$pval,
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
}
summary(sel_p)
mean(sel_p <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)   # close to 0.05, unlike the naive test
```

Side by side, the contrast is stark:

```{r compare}
data.frame(
  test            = c("naive", "selective"),
  mean_pvalue     = c(mean(naive_p, na.rm = TRUE), mean(sel_p, na.rm = TRUE)),
  reject_at_0.05  = c(mean(naive_p <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                      mean(sel_p   <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
)
```

## A brief power illustration

Calibration on the null is only useful if the test still has power when there
is *real* structure. Here we generate three well-separated Gaussian blobs at
the vertices of a triangle, so any pair of recovered clusters genuinely differs
in mean. The selective test should now reject.

```{r power}
make_separated <- function(delta = 6) {
  centers <- matrix(c(0, 0, delta, 0, delta / 2, delta), 3, 2, byrow = TRUE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(j) {
    matrix(stats::rnorm(12 * 2), 12, 2) +
      matrix(centers[j, ], 12, 2, byrow = TRUE)
  }))
}

n_rep <- 6
pow_p <- rep(NA_real_, n_rep)
for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {
  Xr  <- make_separated()
  clr <- kmeans_fun(Xr, k = 3)$cluster
  tb  <- sort(table(clr), decreasing = TRUE)
  k1  <- as.integer(names(tb)[1]); k2 <- as.integer(names(tb)[2])
  pow_p[r] <- selective_hotelling_test(
    Xr, k1, k2, K = 3, sampler = "fast",
    burn = 200, B = 400, thin = 2
  )$pval
}
pow_p
mean(pow_p <= 0.05)   # high power: separated clusters are detected
```

The selective p-values are at or near the Monte Carlo floor, so the test
detects the true separation essentially every time -- it controls selective
Type I error on the null **and** retains power against genuine cluster
differences.

## Practical notes

- Use `condition_on = "final"` (the default) for inference. The
  `"trajectory"` option is **experimental**: its feasible region is much
  tighter and the local sampler under-mixes there.
- The MCMC settings here (`burn = 200`, `B = 400`, `thin = 2`) are tuned for a
  fast vignette. For real analyses, increase them (e.g. `burn = 1000`,
  `B = 2000`, `thin = 5`) and inspect `summary()` for the acceptance rate and
  number of unique draws.
- See `?selective_hotelling_test` for the available samplers (`"fast"`,
  `"har"`, `"cayley"`) and all arguments.

## References

- Chen, Y. T. and Witten, D. M. (2023). Selective inference for k-means
  clustering. *Journal of Machine Learning Research*.
- Gao, L. L., Bien, J. and Witten, D. (2024). Selective inference for
  hierarchical clustering. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*.
